Obviously, before streaming took over, the music industry relied heavily on physical CDs, which had to be manufactured and shipped weeks ahead of their release dates.
But in the mid-'90s and early '00s, that process created an unexpected vulnerability, since factory workers could access albums long before they reached stores, and leak them online. , who was an employee at Kings Mountain, a CD manufacturing plant in North Carolina. Over time, Glover is believed to have been involved in leaking roughly 2,000 albums, including major releases from some of the biggest artists of that time, like Jay-Z, Ashanti, Blink-182, Eminem, U2, Mariah Carey, and Fall Out Boy. The idea of an"EGOT" or"EGOTing" existed before it became part of mainstream pop culture, but it wasn't something most people or even celebs talked about regularly. The term, of course, refers to winning an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony, and it was originally coined in 1984 byThe show treated EGOTing like a goal people actively chase, which helped make the term feel more real and widely understood.
After those episodes aired, the term started showing up more often in entertainment journalism and pop culture conversations. In the film, Gable casually removes his dress shirt without wearing an undershirt underneath, which surprised audiences at the time. According to the legend, men immediately stopped buying undershirts after seeing it.
But the reality is a bit moreThe movie came out during the Great Depression, when many people were already cutting back on nonessential clothing purchases, which likely affected sales. There's also evidence that men's fashion was already shifting, with some moving away from undershirts before the film was even released. Gable himselfdidn't wear undershirts in real life, which is why he didn't wear one in the movie.
While undershirt sales might have dropped, they jumped right back after the start of WWII, when they were part of military uniforms. After the war, many men kept wearing them, and they became a casual staple, especially in the '50s. Chicken nuggets feel like a longtime staple, but they’re actually a ~fairly~ recent invention.
They were first developed in 1963 by, a food science professor at Cornell University who was looking for new ways to make processed chicken more practical and appealing. At the time, Americans didn't eat much chicken, with one reason being that they were usually only sold whole. His method made it possible to form ground chicken into uniform pieces that could be breaded and cooked efficiently without falling apart.
For years, the idea stayed mostly within the food industry rather than becoming a household favorite.and brought them to a national audience. The fast-food giant had originally toyed with fried onions before landing on fried chicken. Their timing lined up with a broader shift in American eating habits that started in the late '70s, that saw many consumers begin moving away from red meat and toward chicken.
This helped turn chicken nuggets from a niche innovation into a very popular food item, especially among children! But that plan changed when Warner Bros. caught wind and stepped in, because it wanted to save that milestone for its upcoming TV series.
With that storyline suddenly off the table, the writers had to come up with a major replacement event on short notice. It followed Grumpy and Dopey on a quest into the Old Forest to the city of Dwarfenholme; along the way, they would meet the other Dwarfs and befriend a young girl named Narcissa. Also, during the journey, the Dwarfs are being hunted by an evil wizard who wants to use them to get the Olden Dwarf’s ancient magical power. But Narcissa is actually the wizard's daughter and works with him to trick the Dwarfs.
The film would have ended with Narcissa double-crossing her father by stealing the Olden Dwarf's magic and placing him in the mirror before turning on the Dwarfs. The idea that police officers are always eating donuts didn't just appear out of nowhere; the trope actually dates back to the mid-20th century. In the 1950s, most restaurants closed early, leaving few places open for officers working overnight shifts.
Donut shops, however, stayed open late or even all night, making them one of the only spots where cops could grab coffee, food, and take a break. These shops also became informal spaces where officers could write reports, talk with other cops, and keep an eye on the neighborhood. This also led to police cars parked outside donut shops late at night becoming a common sight.
Over time, people began to associate cops with donuts because of this, and the association became a pop culture stereotype. And lastly, back in the late '90s, Marvel Entertainment was in serious financial trouble and had just emerged from bankruptcy. To stay afloat, the company started selling off movie rights to its characters to different studios. In 1998, Sony Pictures was offered a deal that reportedly included the rights to a pretty large portion of Marvel's character catalog.
But instead of buying everything, Sony focused on just one character they believed had the most value:. At the time, Spider-Man was Marvel's most recognizable and commercially proven hero, while many other characters weren't yet seen as major box-office draws. Sony passed on the broader deal and secured the film rights to Spider-Man and related characters instead.that allowed both studios to share the character.
Instead of bringing in Tobey Maguire or Andrew Garfield to reprise the role, the studios decided to relaunch with Tom Holland and introduce that version into the MCU.
